power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To investigate the first research question (RQ1), i.e., the psychometric properties of the German PTT-A version, we ran a CFA model, in which all 14 items (or all 6 items for the short version) loaded on a single factor representing PTT-A. Additionally, we also ran the same model in the English sample to again verify the psychometric properties of the original version. Absolute model fit was evaluated using robust RMSEA (Savalei, 2018; Steiger, 1990) and SRMR as descriptive fit indices. As is common practice, we did not interpret the scaled chi-square test -and thus the pvalue -as an indication of unacceptable model fit due the high power statical power. Specifically, a post-hoc power analysis using the R-package SemPower (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) revealed a power of over 95% to detect even minor deviations from perfect fit (e.g., RMSEA = .03 for the smallest subsample of n = 787). Moreover, the CFI and TLI (Bentler, 1990) were not considered indicators of absolute model fit because they are more strongly influenced by loading magnitude than by model misspecification (Moshagen & Auerswald, 2018; van Laar & Braeken, 2022).
table.header: Evaluating the psychometric properties of the German version (RQ1)

table.text: Evaluation of measurement invariance was subsequently conducted by examining changes in relevant fit indices between the different levels of invariance in a multigroup CFA. For this, we examined changes in robust CFI (ΔCFI) 2, robust RMSEA (ΔRMSEA), and robust McDonald's noncentrality index (ΔMc; McDonald, 1989; see Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021), as these indices have been shown in simulation studies on measurement invariance to be particularly informative (Chen, 2007; Cheung & Rensvold, 2002; Meade et al., 2008). Consistent with established guidelines for identifying non-invariance (Chen, 2007; Cheung & Rensvold, 2002), we interpreted ΔCFI < -.01, ΔRMSEA > .015, and ΔMc < -.02 as reflecting a meaningful deterioration in model fit and, consequently, evidence against invariance. Again, we did not interpret the scaled chi-square difference test (Satorra & Bentler, 2010) -and thus the p-value -as an indication of a violation of invariance due the high power statical power. Specifically, a post-hoc power analysis using the Rpackage SemPower (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) revealed a power > 99% to detect neglectable differences in model fit (e.g., ΔRMSEA = .001). We still report the statistics for transparency reasons. 2 Although the usefulness of the CFI for evaluating absolute model fit has been questioned, it remains informative for assessing comparative model fit, as in this context models are evaluated relative to the same reference model Moshagen and Auerswald (2018).

Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) scale by Scholz et al. (2025) provides a psychometrically sound instrument for assessing individual differences in the propensity to trust in automated systems.
text.formatted: The Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) scale by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Scholz et al. (2025)</ref> provides a psychometrically sound instrument for assessing individual differences in the propensity to trust in automated systems.

text.text: To date, however, the scale has only been validated in its original English version.
The present study aimed to validate both the 14-item and 6-item versions of the scale in German.

Furthermore, given the lack of validated measures of PTT-A with established measurement invariance (MI) across languages and gender, we examined whether the scale permits meaningful comparisons across these groups, thereby facilitating cross-cultural research on trust in automation.
To this end, the PTT-A scale was translated into German, and its psychometric properties were evaluated in a large-scale online study (N = 1,629).
In addition to examining the German versions, we assessed the psychometric properties of the original English versions and tested MI across language (English vs.
German) and gender (female vs. male) using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis.
The results supported the psychometric properties of both the 14-item and 6-item versions in English and German.
Furthermore, sufficient MI was established across language and gender, supporting the comparability of scale scores between the respective groups.
Overall, the findings provide a validated German version of the PTT-A scale in both its full and short forms.
The evidence for MI across language and gender further supports its use in cross-language research and comparisons of propensity to trust in automation across these groups.
Recently, Scholz et al. (2025) introduced a new scale to assess the Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) 1 .
text.formatted: Recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Scholz et al. (2025)</ref> introduced a new scale to assess the Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> .

text.text: In their article, they argued that most existing PTT-A measures lack a clear theoretical conceptualization of (the propensity to) trust.

To address this limitation, they proposed a conceptual framework for PTT-A that builds on established models of the propensity to trust (e.g., (Kraus, 2020; McKnight et al., 2002; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2015) across different domains (i.e., trust in other humans, organizational trust, trust in automation).
text.formatted: To address this limitation, they proposed a conceptual framework for PTT-A that builds on established models of the propensity to trust (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kraus, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">McKnight et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2015)</ref> across different domains (i.e., trust in other humans, organizational trust, trust in automation).

text.text: Specifically, they conceptualized PTT-A as (a) a domain-specific manifestation of the general propensity to trust (in humans) (b) based on beliefs of competence, benevolence, and integrity, as well as a trusting stance (c) a stable dispositional trait.

Accordingly, they defined PTT-A as "as the general willingness to rely on automated technology based on Generalized Trustworthiness Expectations and a Trusting Stance towards them" (Scholz et al., 2025, p. 975).
text.formatted: Accordingly, they defined PTT-A as "as the general willingness to rely on automated technology based on Generalized Trustworthiness Expectations and a Trusting Stance towards them" <ref type="bibr">(Scholz et al., 2025, p. 975)</ref>.

text.text: Based on this conceptualization, they argued that existing PTT-A measures do not adequately capture the construct and therefore developed a new scale grounded in established measures of the propensity to trust in humans, as well as automation.

To this end, based on the theoretical assumptions of the integrated trust propensity conceptualization, previously published items were mapped onto these facets and supplemented with newly developed items where suitable items were not available.
Overall, their theoretical assumptions were largely supported.
Across three independent samples, the scale demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, including good model fit, high internal consistency, and satisfactory test-retest reliability.
Furthermore, convergent and discriminant validity was supported by a deductively derived nomological network.
This network comprised basic personality traits as antecedents of PTT-A and trust intentions as its consequences.
To date, the scale has been validated only in its original English version.
Thus, the primary aim of the present study was to develop and validate a German translation of the instrument.
Moreover, we wanted to investigate whether the PTT-A scale offers measurement invariance (MI) across language and gender.
MI is an important prerequisite when comparing observed means between groups (see Dong & Dumas, 2020; Maassen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: MI is an important prerequisite when comparing observed means between groups (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dong & Dumas, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Maassen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: MI refers to the extent to which a measurement instrument assesses the same latent construct in the same way across different groups (e.g., language versions or genders).

Establishing MI is essential because, without it, observed differences in scale scores may reflect differences in the measurement properties of the instrument rather than true differences in the underlying construct.
Consequently, comparisons of observed scores across groups may be misleading and lead to erroneous conclusions (Dong & Dumas, 2020; Steinmetz, 2013).
text.formatted: Consequently, comparisons of observed scores across groups may be misleading and lead to erroneous conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dong & Dumas, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Steinmetz, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, despite its central role in methodological research, measurement invariance has received relatively little attention in the literature on PTT-A, or even propensity to trust in general (Tan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Importantly, despite its central role in methodological research, measurement invariance has received relatively little attention in the literature on PTT-A, or even propensity to trust in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, there is a clear need for a PTT-A measure whose crosslanguage MI has been systematically evaluated.
Such evidence would substantially strengthen confidence in multilingual research employing the scale.
Similarly, a further aim was to examine measurement invariance across gender.
Previous studies have not consistently supported gender differences in propensity to trust automation (e.g., Merritt & Ilgen, 2008; Montag et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Previous studies have not consistently supported gender differences in propensity to trust automation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Merritt & Ilgen, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Montag et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, interpreting either observed differences or their absence requires evidence that the instrument measures the construct comparably across groups.
Examining measurement invariance across genders therefore provides an important basis for meaningful comparisons.
As such, we evaluated the psychometric properties of the PTT-A scale in an online study (total N = 1,629) assessing the PPT-A scale an English and German speaking sample respectively.
Accordingly, the present study addressed the following research questions:
RQ2: Does the scale demonstrate (partial) measurement invariance across its English and German language versions?
RQ3: Does the scale demonstrate (partial) measurement invariance across gender (male vs. female)?

Participants were drawn from darkfactor.org, a publicly available platform providing free, anonymous assessments of socially and/or ethically aversive personality traits along with personalized feedback.
Recruitment was not targeted toward specific demographic groups.
Rather, the platform is accessed on an ongoing basis by individuals who learn about it through media coverage, word of mouth, recommendations from others, and other sources.
Consequently, the resulting samples encompass participants with diverse demographic backgrounds.
All studies adhered to established ethical guidelines and involved no deception.

The data collection procedures were reviewed and approved by the institutional review board (IRB) of the RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau, Department of Psychology (approval numbers LEK-154 and LEK-567).
Data quality was assessed using a set of pre-specified validity checks.
Participants were removed from the analyses when they met criteria indicating, for example, excessively rapid responding, flatlining, or low credibility of their responses.
These exclusion criteria were established a priori and are applied uniformly across all studies using a sample from the website.
A detailed description of the criteria and their implementation is provided at https://osf.io/93tw6/?view_only=7f95882ef704429f866039350fc25baf.
text.formatted: A detailed description of the criteria and their implementation is provided at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/93tw6/?view_only=7f95882ef704429f866039350fc25baf">https://osf.io/93tw6/?view_only=7f95882ef704429f866039350fc25baf</ref>.

text.text: Following popular recommendations to ensure model convergence and identification (Jackson, 2003; Kyriazos, 2018), minimum sample sizes per language were set heuristically to n = 20 per item.
text.formatted: Following popular recommendations to ensure model convergence and identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Jackson, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kyriazos, 2018)</ref>, minimum sample sizes per language were set heuristically to n = 20 per item.

text.text: The resulting samples were larger than this threshold, as sample sizes were primarily determined by participant availability during the respective data-collection periods.
Data collection took place between May and June 2026.
The final sample size is N = 1,629 (nEnglish = 842; nGerman = 787).
Demographic data of both samples are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: Demographic data of both samples are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: After providing informed consent, participants answered questions not relevant to the current study for which they were offered to obtain personalized feedback.
They were subsequently asked to confirm that they had responded sincerely and to indicate whether they agreed to the use of their data for scientific research.
Participants then reported basic demographic information and were offered the option of answering additional questions prior to receiving personalized personality feedback.
It was made clear that completing these follow-up measures was voluntary and that personalized feedback would be provided regardless of whether participants chose to answer them.
Those who opted to continue completed the PTT-A scale in either English or German.
No further compensation or other incentives were offered for completing the PTT-A scale.
Propensity to trust in automated technology (PTT-A) was assessed using the 14-item PTT-A scale developed by Scholz et al. (2025).
text.formatted: Propensity to trust in automated technology (PTT-A) was assessed using the 14-item PTT-A scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Scholz et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: The scale assesses individuals' general tendency to trust automated technology, with items covering beliefs regarding the competence, benevolence, and integrity of automated technology, as well as a general trusting stance.
The scale offers a balanced number of positively and negatively keyed items and is rated on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
The scale demonstrated adequate model fit and high reliability across two samples.
It also demonstrated good test-retest reliability over approximately one year and, based on a theoretical derived nomological network, evidence for convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity.
Note that the authors also provided a shorter, 6-item version of the scale, which we also investigate herein.
For the German version, we used a back-translation procedure (Brislin, 1970).
text.formatted: For the German version, we used a back-translation procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brislin, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Following recently proposed procedures (Andersen et al., 2026; Chung & Kim, 2025; Kunst & Bierwiaczonek, 2023), the translation process was supported by artificial intelligence.
text.formatted: Following recently proposed procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andersen et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Chung & Kim, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kunst & Bierwiaczonek, 2023)</ref>, the translation process was supported by artificial intelligence.

text.text: Specifically, the original English items were provided to Perplexity (Grok 4.1; Perplexity AI, 2026) using the following prompt: "Please translate the following items from a psychological scale into German: [followed by the items]."
The resulting translation was independently reviewed by two native German speakers for comprehensibility and correspondence with the content of the original items.

The reviewers agreed on a final German version, which was then back-translated into English using another AI system, ChatGPT (GPT-5.5; OpenAI, 2026), with the following prompt: "Please translate the following items from a psychological scale into English: [followed by the items]."
The back-translated items were compared with the original English items.
All back-translated items were nearly identical to the original items, indicating a high degree of correspondence between the original and translated versions.
The translation was therefore considered satisfactory.

To investigate the first research question (RQ1), i.e., the psychometric properties of the German PTT-A version, we ran a CFA model, in which all 14 items (or all 6 items for the short version) loaded on a single factor representing PTT-A. Additionally, we also ran the same model in the English sample to again verify the psychometric properties of the original version.
Absolute model fit was evaluated using robust RMSEA (Savalei, 2018; Steiger, 1990) and SRMR as descriptive fit indices.
text.formatted: Absolute model fit was evaluated using robust RMSEA <ref type="bibr">(Savalei, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Steiger, 1990)</ref> and SRMR as descriptive fit indices.

text.text: As is common practice, we did not interpret the scaled chi-square test -and thus the pvalue -as an indication of unacceptable model fit due the high power statical power.

Specifically, a post-hoc power analysis using the R-package SemPower (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) revealed a power of over 95% to detect even minor deviations from perfect fit (e.g., RMSEA = .03 for the smallest subsample of n = 787).
text.formatted: Specifically, a post-hoc power analysis using the R-package SemPower <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Moshagen & Bader, 2024)</ref> revealed a power of over 95% to detect even minor deviations from perfect fit (e.g., RMSEA = .03 for the smallest subsample of n = 787).

text.text: Moreover, the CFI and TLI (Bentler, 1990) were not considered indicators of absolute model fit because they are more strongly influenced by loading magnitude than by model misspecification (Moshagen & Auerswald, 2018; van Laar & Braeken, 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, the CFI and TLI <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bentler, 1990)</ref> were not considered indicators of absolute model fit because they are more strongly influenced by loading magnitude than by model misspecification <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Moshagen & Auerswald, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">van Laar & Braeken, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, all indices are reported for transparency.

Following common conventions, RMSEA values < .06 and SRMR values < .08 were considered indicative of good fit, whereas RMSEA values < .10 and SRMR values < .11 were considered indicative of acceptable fit (Browne & Cudeck, 1992; Hu & Bentler, 1999).
text.formatted: Following common conventions, RMSEA values < .06 and SRMR values < .08 were considered indicative of good fit, whereas RMSEA values < .10 and SRMR values < .11 were considered indicative of acceptable fit <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Browne & Cudeck, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hu & Bentler, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: We relied on McDonald's omega (ꞷ; McDonald, 1999) as a measure of reliability.

To examine the other two research questions, i.e., whether the scale has measurement invariance (MI) across languages (RQ2) and gender (RQ3) respectively, we followed the recommended approach when testing for MI (Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021; L. Milfont & Fischer, 2010; Meredith, 1993).
text.formatted: To examine the other two research questions, i.e., whether the scale has measurement invariance (MI) across languages (RQ2) and gender (RQ3) respectively, we followed the recommended approach when testing for MI <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">L. Milfont & Fischer, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Meredith, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, MI is typically evaluated in a hierarchical sequence comprising four increasingly restrictive levels of invariance: Configural invariance.
Configural invariance tests whether the same factor structure holds across groups.

If configural invariance cannot be established, this suggests that the construct is indicated by an unequal number of latent variables across groups, meaning that that the construct is conceptualized or represented differently across groups.
Metric (or weak) invariance.
Metric invariance tests whether factor loadings are equivalent across groups.
In other words, it examines whether the items are equally strongly related to the underlying latent construct in each group.
If metric invariance is violated, some items may be more informative indicators of the construct in one group (e.g., one language version) than in another.
Establishing metric invariance permits meaningful comparisons of associations involving the latent construct (e.g., latent correlations or regression coefficients) across groups.
Scalar (strong) invariance.
Scalar invariance tests whether item intercepts are equivalent across groups.
If scalar invariance is not supported, systematic differences in observed item scores may reflect measurement artifacts rather than true differences in the latent construct.
For example, respondents from one group may consistently endorse certain items more strongly despite having the same latent trait level.
Establishing scalar invariance allows meaningful comparisons of latent means across groups.
Strict invariance.
Strict invariance additionally requires equality of item residual variances across groups.
If this assumption is violated, the reliability or measurement precision of individual items differs between groups.
Establishing strict invariance supports comparisons based on observed (manifest) scale scores.
In practice, establishing full scalar or even full strict invariance is relatively uncommon (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016; Schmitt & Kuljanin, 2008).
text.formatted: In practice, establishing full scalar or even full strict invariance is relatively uncommon <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Putnick & Bornstein, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schmitt & Kuljanin, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A recent systematic review revealed that none of the 75 studies examined achieved full scalar or strict MI across different nations and less than half achieved those for gender (Dong & Dumas, 2020).
text.formatted: A recent systematic review revealed that none of the 75 studies examined achieved full scalar or strict MI across different nations and less than half achieved those for gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dong & Dumas, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, even well-established personality inventories, such as the HEXACO-100 (Lee & Ashton, 2018) or the Dark Factor of Personality (D; Moshagen et al., 2018), often contain a substantial proportion of items (> 33%) that do not exhibit invariance across languages (see Bader, Horsten, et al., 2021; Pischel & Hilbig, 2026; Thielmann et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Indeed, even well-established personality inventories, such as the HEXACO-100 <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Lee & Ashton, 2018)</ref> or the Dark Factor of Personality (D; <ref type="bibr">Moshagen et al., 2018)</ref>, often contain a substantial proportion of items (> 33%) that do not exhibit invariance across languages (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bader, Horsten, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pischel & Hilbig, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Thielmann et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we interpret partial invariance of less than 33% of items as an indication of sufficient MI.
Evaluation of measurement invariance was subsequently conducted by examining changes in relevant fit indices between the different levels of invariance in a multigroup CFA.

For this, we examined changes in robust CFI (ΔCFI) 2 , robust RMSEA (ΔRMSEA), and robust McDonald's noncentrality index (ΔMc; McDonald, 1989; see Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021), as these indices have been shown in simulation studies on measurement invariance to be particularly informative (Chen, 2007; Cheung & Rensvold, 2002; Meade et al., 2008).

text.text: In a first step, we identified the equally constraint on the intercept of item #7 as the greatest source of misfit.
As freeing this parameter still led to considerable misfit, we also freed the equality constraint on the intercept of item #14.
This led to acceptable differences in the fit indies.
Strict invariance was also supported by the data.

In sum, this means that sufficient MI was achieved, as the equality constraints on the intercepts of only two items (14% of the 14-item scale, thus below the a-priori set threshold of 33%) had to be relaxed.
Regarding the 6-item version, configural MI was supported.
We had to loosen the equality constraint of the loading and intercept item #7 to achieve partial metric and partial scalar MI respectively.
Strict MI was fully supported.
In sum, this means that sufficient MI was achieved, as the equality constraints on the loading and intercept of only one item (17% of the 6-item scale) had to be relaxed.

With the present study, we developed and evaluated a German version of the Propensity to
Trust in Automation (PTT-A) scale, a measure for the dispositional tendency to trust automated technology, such as robots and AI systems.
Across English-and German-speaking samples, the full 14-item version of the PTT-A scale demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, including adequate to good model fit and high reliability.

The abbreviated 6-item version performed well in both the English and the German sample (in the English sample even better than in the original study), yielding it a good alternative if the 14-item version is not feasible.
A particular contribution of the present study is the systematic examination of measurement invariance (MI).
Despite its importance for meaningful comparisons across groups, MI is rarely examined in applied psychological research.
For example, only 4% of the 96 articles reviewed by Maassen et al. (2025) reported tests of MI.
text.formatted: For example, only 4% of the 96 articles reviewed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Maassen et al. (2025)</ref> reported tests of MI.

text.text: Similarly, MI has received little attention in research on propensity to trust (Tan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, MI has received little attention in research on propensity to trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although Tan et al. (2025) demonstrated (partial) MI for a measure of the general propensity to trust in other humans, we are not aware of previous evidence for MI of a measure of PTT-A. This is important because ignoring violations of MI can bias comparisons based on composite scores such as manifest means (Guenole & Brown, 2014; Steinmetz, 2013).

text.text: Across the two language versions, full configural and metric invariance were supported, whereas scalar invariance required relaxing equality constraints for two items, corresponding to 14% of the scale.
Strict invariance was subsequently supported.

Importantly, full scalar or strict variance is usually not achieved (Dong & Dumas, 2020) and this proportion of non-invariant items is comparable to that reported for established personality inventories (e.g., HEXACO-100, Thielmann et al., 2020; or Dark Factor of Personality, Bader, Horsten, et al., 2021; Pischel & Hilbig, 2026).

text.text: We thus conclude that the scale shows sufficient (partial) MI across the examined languages.
The 6-item version performed similarly well, with only one out of six items (17%) being non-invariant (regarding loading and intercept), thus also achieving sufficient partial MI.
Moreover, both PTT-A scale versions turned out to show full MI regarding gender (male vs. female).
The findings have several practical implications.
First, full measurement invariance was supported across gender.
Accordingly, comparisons of manifest PTT-A scores between male and female participants can be meaningfully interpreted.

This finding provides a methodological basis for investigating potential gender differences in the propensity to trust automation without conflating such differences with differences in the measurement properties of the scale.
Second, comparisons across the English and German versions require somewhat greater caution, as only partial MI could be achieved.

In contexts in which latent-variable modeling is not feasible, the use of manifest means may nevertheless be considered, particularly given that the extent of non-invariance is relatively small and comparable to that observed in established personality measures.

Previous methodological work has discussed the use of manifest scores under partial invariance, particularly when the degree of non-invariance is limited (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002; Steenkamp & Baumgartner, 1998; Vandenberg & Lance, 2000).

text.text: Nevertheless, whenever feasible, comparisons based on latent means are preferable because they allow measurement error and the identified non-invariance to be modeled explicitly (Dong & Dumas, 2020).

text.text: Researchers using the PTT-A for cross-language comparisons should therefore consider latent-variable approaches when these are feasible.

Taken together, the presented German versions of the PTTA scale (full and short version) showed good psychometric properties in this study and offer validated and economic tools for assessing the individual disposition to trust automated technology for both scientific and practical settings.

A strength of the present study is the relatively large overall sample (N = 1,629) and the heterogeneity of participants recruited through a publicly available assessment platform rather than a narrowly defined demographic population.
Nevertheless, the samples were self-selected and cannot be assumed to be representative of the broader English-and German-speaking populations.
Future research should therefore examine the PTT-A in more representative samples and across additional demographic and cultural groups.
Finally, although the present findings provide evidence for cross-language comparability, language and cultural context were not experimentally separable.
Differences between the English-and German-speaking samples may therefore reflect linguistic or cultural characteristics.
Further research may adopt the Culture, Comprehension, and Translation Bias (CCT; Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021) to further examine the source of MI.
text.formatted: Further research may adopt the Culture, Comprehension, and Translation Bias (CCT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bader, Jobst, et al., 2021)</ref> to further examine the source of MI.

text.text: In conclusion, the present study provides a German version of the PTT-A with satisfactory psychometric properties and evidence for the scale's MI across language and gender.
The scale can therefore be used to assess the dispositional tendency to trust automated technology in both English-and German-speaking contexts and for investigating gender differences.
